claim: Myxobacteria exchange large amounts of outer membrane lipids and proteins upon contact through outer membrane exchange (OME).
source: Myxobacteria are known for complex social behaviors including outer membrane exchange (OME), in which cells exchange large amounts of outer membrane lipids and proteins upon contact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: The TraA cell surface receptor selects OME partners based on a variable domain.
source: The TraA cell surface receptor selects OME partners based on a variable domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: traA polymorphism alone is not sufficient to precisely discriminate kin.
source: However, traA polymorphism alone is not sufficient to precisely discriminate kin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing that some non-kin genotypes share compatible traA alleles.

claim: SitA lipoprotein toxins are polymorphic and widespread in myxobacteria.
source: These SitA lipoprotein toxins are polymorphic and widespread in myxobacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by bioinformatic analysis showing >100 sitA orthologs common in the Myxococcales.

claim: Each sitA is associated with a cognate sitI immunity gene.
source: Each sitA is associated with a cognate sitI immunity gene, and in some cases a sitB accessory gene.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic analysis and competition experiments.

claim: SitA is transferred serially between target cells, allowing the toxins to move cell-to-cell like an infectious agent.
source: Remarkably, we show that SitA is transferred serially between target cells, allowing the toxins to move cell-to-cell like an infectious agent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through three-strain competition experiments and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: SitA toxins define strong identity barriers between strains.
source: Consequently, SitA toxins define strong identity barriers between strains and likely contribute to population structure, maintenance of cooperation, and strain diversification.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by colony merger assays showing demarcation zones between strains expressing different sitAI cassettes.

claim: OME occurs constitutively on surfaces and facilitates efficient OM homogenization of populations with heterogeneous OMs.
source: This process occurs constitutively on surfaces and facilitates efficient OM homogenization of populations with heterogeneous OMs (Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Nearly all recipient cells receive substantial amounts of cargo protein within two hours of co-culture during OME.
source: Exchange of fluorescent OM lipoprotein reporters, as well as endogenous OM lipoproteins, demonstrates that nearly all recipient cells receive substantial amounts of cargo protein within two hours of co-culture (Nudleman et al., 2005; Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Cells with lethal defects in lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis can be sustained in a population by OME with wild-type donors.
source: Furthermore, cells with lethal defects in lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis can be sustained in a population by OME with wild-type (WT) donors (Vassallo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: TraA has a variable domain that specifies recognition between cells through homotypic interactions.
source: In this regard, we previously showed that TraA has a variable domain that specifies recognition between cells through homotypic interactions (Pathak et al., 2013; Cao and Wall, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Myxobacteria with divergent, incompatible TraA receptors do not engage in OME.
source: Thus, myxobacteria with divergent, incompatible TraA receptors do not engage in OME.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by prior citations.

claim: Some non-kin genotypes share compatible traA alleles.
source: Indeed, although TraA sequence diversity in the variable domain is high, some non-kin genotypes share compatible traA alleles (Pathak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Some Myxococcus isolates that antagonize one another in co-culture possess the same traA alleles.
source: In fact, some Myxococcus isolates that antagonize one another in co-culture possess the same traA alleles (Pathak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: There are additional genetic determinants beyond traA that more precisely discriminate kin during social interactions.
source: Based on this observation, we hypothesized that there are additional genetic determinants that more precisely discriminate kin during social interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction based on prior observations.

claim: Bacterial kin discrimination is often mediated by antagonism toward non-kin through delivery of polymorphic toxins between cells in close contact.
source: Bacterial kin discrimination is often mediated by antagonism toward non-kin. One mechanism that bacteria use to this end is the delivery of polymorphic toxins between cells in close contact (Zhang et al., 2012; Ruhe et al., 2013; Cardarelli et al., 2015; Wenren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Polymorphic toxins usually share homology in species-specific amino-terminal domains required for presentation and/or delivery, but vary in their carboxy-terminal toxin domains.
source: These toxins usually share homology in species-specific amino-terminal domains required for presentation and/or delivery, but vary in their carboxy-terminal toxin domains (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Each polymorphic toxin is associated with a cognate immunity protein, typically encoded together in an operon, which specifically neutralizes toxicity in the producing cell and in clonemates or close kin that share the locus.
source: Each toxin is associated with a cognate immunity protein, typically encoded together in an operon, which specifically neutralizes toxicity in the producing cell and in clonemates or close kin that share the locus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The DK1622 reference strain of M. xanthus is killed by ancestral strains when co-cultured on surfaces.
source: We previously showed that the widely used DK1622 reference strain of M. xanthus is killed by ancestral strains when co-cultured on surfaces (Dey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: A traA mutation in either strain abolishes antagonism between DK1622 and ancestral strains.
source: A traA mutation in either strain abolishes this behavior, indicating that OME is required for antagonism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Antagonism between DK1622 and ancestral strains requires a hyper-variable region of the chromosome called Mx-alpha.
source: Further, this antagonism requires a hyper-variable region of the chromosome called Mx-alpha, which is composed of roughly 100 kb of prophage and mobile genetic elements and can be found in multiple copies of imperfect repeats in M. xanthus genomes (Dey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Ancestral strains that antagonize DK1622 have three homologous Mx-alpha units apparently arranged in tandem.
source: In ancestral strains that antagonize DK1622, there are three homologous Mx-alpha units apparently arranged in tandem.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Two Mx-alpha units (~200 kb) were lost by spontaneous deletion during the construction of DK1622.
source: However, two of these units (~200 kb) were lost by spontaneous deletion during the construction of DK1622 (Dey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: SitA1 is encoded by gene MXF1DRAFT_07513 on Mx-alpha.
source: Sequence analysis of the two Mx-alpha units retained in the ancestral DK101 strain (a.k.a. DZF1) (Müller et al., 2013) but lost in DK1622 revealed a candidate toxin gene (MXF1DRAFT_07513), which we have designated sitA1 for swarm inhibition toxin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the identification of SitA1.

claim: SitA1 is a predicted lipoprotein that contains a C-terminal nuclease domain with a WHH motif.
source: This gene encodes a predicted lipoprotein that contains a C-terminal nuclease domain with a WHH motif (Zhang et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The absence of lysine at the +2 position or alanine at the +7 position relative to the +1 cysteine in the N-terminal lipobox suggests that SitA1 is localized to the OM.
source: The absence of lysine at the +2 position or alanine at the +7 position relative to the +1 cysteine in the N-terminal lipobox suggests that this protein is localized to the OM (Bhat et al., 2011) (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to prior work on lipoprotein localization.

claim: sitI1 is located immediately downstream of sitA1 and shows homology to the SUKH-family of immunity proteins.
source: Immediately downstream of sitA1 is a gene (sitI1) that shows homology to the SUKH-family of immunity proteins commonly found in polymorphic toxin systems (Zhang et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: sitB1 is located upstream of sitA1 and is a hypothetical gene of unknown function.
source: Upstream of sitA1 is a hypothetical gene (sitB1) of unknown function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The sitB1 ORF overlaps with sitA1 by 11 base pairs, suggesting that the genes form an operon and function together.
source: The sitB1 ORF overlaps with sitA1 by 11 base pairs, suggesting that the genes form an operon and function together (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Nonmotile ancestral cells inhibited the motility of DK1622, but not the DK1622 ∆traA strain.
source: As shown previously (Pathak et al., 2013; Dey et al., 2016; Dey and Wall, 2014), nonmotile ancestral cells inhibited the motility of DK1622, but not the DK1622 ∆traA strain (Figure 1B, rows 1–4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: Nonmotile ancestors carrying a sitA1 mutation did not inhibit DK1622.
source: Importantly, nonmotile ancestors carrying a sitA1 mutation did not inhibit DK1622 (Figure 1B, row 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of sitI1 in motile DK1622 cells prevented antagonism by nonmotile ancestors.
source: Further, expression of sitI1 in motile DK1622 cells also prevented antagonism (Figure 1B, row 6), consistent with the prediction that sitI encodes an immunity protein that neutralizes SitA1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Ectopic sitBAI1 expression in nonmotile ∆Mx-alpha cells allowed them to inhibit DK1622.
source: As predicted, ectopic sitBAI1 expression allowed the nonmotile ∆Mx-alpha cells to inhibit DK1622, thus recapitulating the antagonistic phenotype exhibited by the nonmotile ancestor strain (Figure 1B, rows 7–8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The loss of two Mx-alpha units, and thus the sitBAI1 operon, during the construction of DK1622 from an ancestral DK101 strain explains why the latter strain antagonizes the former.
source: Therefore, the loss of two Mx-alpha units, and thus the sitBAI1 operon (Figure 2A), during the construction of DK1622 from an ancestral DK101 strain explains why the latter strain antagonizes the former.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Strain DK101 carries three Mx-alpha repeats, whereas DK1622 retains only one copy.
source: Strain DK101 (the ancestor of DK1622) carries three Mx-alpha repeats, whereas DK1622 retains only one copy.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2A caption and shown in the figure.

claim: Each Mx-alpha unit contains a unique sitBAI cassette.
source: Each Mx-alpha unit contains a unique sitBAI cassette.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2A caption and shown in the figure.

claim: sitBAI-expressing inhibitor cells significantly outcompeted target cells in competition assays.
source: In all instances, sitBAI-expressing inhibitor cells significantly outcompeted target cells, whereas the mock-inhibitor did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A ∆traA mutation in either the target or inhibitor strain abolished the inhibitor's competitive advantage.
source: Furthermore, a ∆traA mutation in either the target or inhibitor strain abolished the inhibitor's competitive advantage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Delivery of SitA1 and SitA2 over a 24 hr period induced filamentation and lysis of target cells.
source: Delivery of SitA1 and SitA2 over a 24 hr period induced filamentation and lysis of target cells, whereas SitA3 induced rounding and lysis of target cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SitA3 induced rounding and lysis of target cells.
source: Delivery of SitA1 and SitA2 over a 24 hr period induced filamentation and lysis of target cells, whereas SitA3 induced rounding and lysis of target cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells expressing a SitA1-mCherry fusion have membrane-localized fluorescence.
source: Cells expressing this fusion have membrane-localized fluorescence as expected for a lipoprotein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The SitA1-mCherry reporter is transferred between cells in a TraA-dependent manner.
source: At 6 hr of co-culture, we observed the mCherry signal present in the cell envelope of the GFP target strain, indicating cell-to-cell transfer of the SitA1-mCherry reporter (Figure 2C, upper panel). Deletion of traA in the GFP target strain prevented the acquisition of mCherry signal (Figure 2C, lower panel), recapitulating our earlier findings that OM-localized reporters are exchanged between cells in a TraA/B-dependent manner (Nudleman et al., 2005; Wei et al., 2011; Pathak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2C and citations to prior work.

claim: Full-length SitA1 localizes to the cell envelope.
source: We confirmed that full-length SitA1 localizes to the cell envelope using immunofluorescence microscopy to detect FLAG epitope-tagged SitA1 in formaldehyde-fixed cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: SitA1 resides in the OM and is transferred cell-to-cell by OME.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that SitA1 resides in the OM and is transferred cell-to-cell by OME.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization and transfer experiments.

claim: For each competition, only strains that express the cognate sitI were protected from growth inhibition.
source: For each competition, only strains that express the cognate sitI were protected from growth inhibition (Figure 2E), consistent with immunity function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Expression of SitA1-CTD and SitA3-CTD blocked E. coli growth, but co-expression of cognate sitI from a second plasmid restored cell growth.
source: Expression of SitA1-CTD and SitA3-CTD blocked growth, but co-expression of cognate sitI from a second plasmid restored cell growth (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: SitI proteins specifically neutralize cognate SitA toxins.
source: These results confirm that SitI proteins specifically neutralize cognate SitA toxins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the E. coli expression experiments.

claim: The SitA-CTD constructs lack secretion signal sequences and exert their toxic effects in the cytoplasm.
source: In addition, because the SitA-CTD constructs lack secretion signal sequences, these data show that the domains exert their toxic effects in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the E. coli expression experiments.

claim: Each SitA-CTD inhibited M. xanthus cell growth when expressed in the cytoplasm.
source: Because SitA2-mediated inhibition is obvious in M. xanthus competition co-cultures (Figure 2B and E), we tested the SitA-CTD expression constructs in M. xanthus and found that each inhibited cell growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SitA2 is not sufficiently potent by itself to block outward swarming of DK1622.
source: This result confirms that SitA2 contributes to the swarm inhibition phenotype, but is not sufficiently potent by itself to block outward swarming of DK1622.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on swarm inhibition assays.

claim: SitA1 is the major swarm-inhibition toxin.
source: Together, these results indicate that SitA1 is the major swarm-inhibition toxin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from swarm inhibition assays.

claim: A nonmotile strain expressing sitBAI3 fully inhibits the motility of a DK1622 ∆sitBAI3 strain that lacks the sitI3 immunity gene.
source: However, we found that a nonmotile strain expressing sitBAI3 fully inhibits the motility of a DK1622 ∆sitBAI3 strain that lacks the sitI3 immunity gene (Figure 1C, row 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Induction of SitA3-CTD expression inhibited E. coli cell growth in the same manner as the CdiA-CTD toxins.
source: Induction of SitA3-CTD expression inhibited cell growth in the same manner as the CdiA-CTD toxins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: SitA3-CTD cleaves tRNAUGCAla, similar to the specific tRNase activity of the B. pseudomallei toxin.
source: Examination of tRNA from SitA3-CTD intoxicated cells revealed cleavage of tRNAUGCAla, similar to the specific tRNase activity of the B. pseudomallei toxin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: E. coli cells expressing sitA1-CTD became filamentous and lost DAPI staining.
source: To test this, we induced SitA1-CTD expression in E. coli and found that cells became filamentous and had reduced DAPI stain signal (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: E. coli cells that were intoxicated by SitA3-CTD retained DAPI staining, though their nucleoids became more compact.
source: By contrast, E. coli cells that were intoxicated by SitA3-CTD retained DAPI staining, though their nucleoids became more compact (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: SitA1-CTD has DNase activity.
source: Together, these results suggest that SitA1-CTD has DNase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the DAPI staining experiments.

claim: Expression of SitA2-CTD in M. xanthus resulted in cell filamentation and reduced DAPI staining.
source: To examine this possibility, we expressed each SitA-CTD in M. xanthus under the control of an IPTG-inducible promoter. Expression of SitA2-CTD in M. xanthus resulted in cell filamentation and reduced DAPI staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that SitA2-CTD degrades DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SitA2-CTD degrades DNA.
source: Expression of SitA2-CTD in M. xanthus resulted in cell filamentation and reduced DAPI staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that SitA2-CTD degrades DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A BLAST search using the N-terminal domains of SitA1/2 and SitA3 as query sequences recovered >100 sitA orthologs that are common in the Myxococcales.
source: To determine the phylogenetic distribution of SitA toxins, we conducted a BLAST search using the N-terminal domains of SitA1/2 (which are homologous) and SitA3 as query sequences. This search recovered >100 sitA orthologs that are common in the Myxococcales (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: All SitA orthologs contain lipoboxes and are only found in species that contain traAB.
source: Consistent with the finding that SitA is delivered through OME, all orthologs contain lipoboxes and are only found in species that contain traAB.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: SitA C-terminal domains are variable and typically show homology to nuclease domains when subjected to HMM-HMM comparison using HHpred.
source: Moreover, SitA C-terminal domains are variable and typically show homology to nuclease domains when subjected to HMM-HMM comparison using HHpred (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Many sitA genes are not linked to upstream sitB orthologs, particularly in species that are distantly related to M. xanthus.
source: Interestingly, many sitA genes are not linked to upstream sitB orthologs, particularly in species that are distantly related to M. xanthus (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: M. xanthus cells that express heterologous sitAI3Mf1 or sitBAI1Mf1 from Myxococcus fulvus HW1 outcompeted the parental strain in a traA-dependent manner.
source: As predicted, M. xanthus cells that express heterologous sitAI3Mf1 or sitBAI1Mf1 outcompeted the parental strain in a traA-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: SitA toxin delivery is not limited by its specific species/strain of origin.
source: These results indicate that SitA toxin delivery is not limited by its specific species/strain of origin, and that the systems are functional after horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of a minimal set of components (sitAI).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the heterologous expression experiments.

claim: Expression of different sitAI cassettes resulted in dramatic lines of demarcation between two strains in colony merger assays.
source: For each combination, the expression of different sitAI cassettes resulted in dramatic lines of demarcation between the two strains (Figure 4A), and the formation of these demarcation zones was traA-dependent (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Otherwise isogenic strains are rendered socially incompatible and geographically isolated by the acquisition of a single sitAI cassette.
source: These results show that otherwise isogenic strains are rendered socially incompatible and geographically isolated by the acquisition of a single sitAI cassette.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the colony merger assays.

claim: Each inhibitor cell intoxicates several thousand target cells during co-culture.
source: These observations imply that each inhibitor cell intoxicates several thousand target cells during co-culture.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the CFU data.

claim: Inclusion of intermediary cells resulted in the inhibition of traABDK1622 target cells in three-strain competitions.
source: Importantly, inclusion of intermediary cells, which are inhibited (Figure 5D), also resulted in the inhibition of traABDK1622 target cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: The intermediary strain (which lacks sitBAI1) did not inhibit traABDK1622 targets in co-cultures containing only those two strains.
source: As expected, the intermediary strain (which lacks sitBAI1) did not inhibit traABDK1622 targets in co-cultures containing only those two strains (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5F.

claim: In three-strain competition with sitI1 immunity in targets, the intermediary strain was inhibited, but traABDK1622 targets were not.
source: To exclude a SitA-independent mechanism of target cell inhibition, we conducted the same three-strain competition, but provided traABDK1622 targets with the sitI1 immunity gene. In this latter co-culture, the intermediary strain was inhibited, but traABDK1622 targets were not (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5G.

claim: An intermediary strain that lacks traA did not result in inhibition of either intermediary or target cells during co-culture.
source: Finally, we tested an intermediary strain that lacks traA and found that neither intermediary nor target cells were inhibited during co-culture (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5H.

claim: All GFP-labeled target cells acquired mCherry fluorescence localized to the cell envelope at 6 hr in three-strain co-cultures with intermediary cells.
source: Microscopic examination of target cells at 6 hr revealed that all had acquired mCherry fluorescence, with the signal localized to the cell envelope (Figure 5I, left panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5I.

claim: No SitA1-mCherry transfer was detected when the intermediary was absent from the co-culture.
source: By contrast, no SitA1-mCherry transfer was detected when the intermediary was absent from the co-culture (Figure 5I, right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5I.

claim: TraA-mCherry fusion promoted efficient transfer of an OM sfGFP reporter.
source: The TraA fusion promoted efficient transfer of an OM sfGFP reporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that it is functional to catalyze OME.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TraA-mCherry itself was not transferred during OME.
source: However, TraA-mCherry itself was not transferred (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SitA1 can be transferred from the initial target to secondary recipients.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that SitA1 can be transferred from the initial target to secondary recipients, supporting a model in which SitA acts like an infectious agent that disseminates through a population by OME.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the three-strain competition and microscopy experiments.

claim: SitB1 contributes significantly to SitA1-mediated inhibition.
source: Thus, SitB1 contributes significantly to SitA1-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from competition experiments comparing sitBAI and sitAI inhibitors.

claim: sitBAI1 cells outcompeted both the intermediary and target strains in three-strain co-cultures.
source: As observed in Figure 5, sitBAI1 cells outcompeted both the intermediary and target strains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: sitAI cells had little to no effect on target cells in three-strain serial transfer assays.
source: Because of the high inhibitor cell ratio, the sitAI1 cells outcompeted the intermediary strain to a similar extent as sitBAI cells, but importantly, sitAI cells had little to no effect on target cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: SitB promotes SitA transfer, including the serial transfer from primary to secondary target cells.
source: These results support the hypothesis that SitB promotes SitA transfer, including the serial transfer from primary to secondary target cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the serial transfer experiments.

claim: Mutant strains that cannot deploy SitA3 had dramatically decreased competitive fitness outcomes and viability compared to WT when co-cultured with environmental isolates.
source: In every case, mutant strains that cannot deploy SitA3 had dramatically decreased competitive fitness outcomes and viability compared to WT (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The ability to deliver SitA3 is a dominant determinant of competitive fitness under co-culture conditions.
source: These results indicate that the ability to deliver SitA3 is a dominant determinant of competitive fitness under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the competition experiments with environmental isolates.

claim: ∆traA cells had less competitive fitness than ∆sitBAI3, indicating a competitive fitness defect in ∆traA cells beyond just the inability to deploy SitA3.
source: Interestingly, these experiments revealed that ∆traA cells had less competitive fitness than ∆sitBAI3, indicating a competitive fitness defect in ∆traA cells beyond just the inability to deploy SitA3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the competition data.

claim: ∆traA and ∆sitBAI3 genotypes resulted in similar competitive outcomes as WT when competed against isolates outside the DK1622 TraA recognition group.
source: ∆traA and ∆sitBAI3 genotypes resulted in similar competitive outcomes as WT as would be expected when inter-strain OME does not occur and SitA3 cannot be deployed (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: SitA contributes significantly to fitness during competition with TraA-compatible non-kin genotypes.
source: These results show that SitA contributes significantly to fitness during competition with TraA-compatible non-kin genotypes, and likely plays a key role in competition and survival in nature.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the competition experiments with environmental isolates.

claim: SitA proteins are similar to other polymorphic toxins in that they carry diverse C-terminal domains, are neutralized by cognate immunity proteins, and are delivered in a cell contact-dependent manner.
source: SitA proteins are similar to other polymorphic toxins in that they carry diverse C-terminal domains, are neutralized by cognate immunity proteins, and are delivered in a cell contact-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: SitA proteins are unique in their N-terminal domains, and in that they are lipoproteins transferred with other cargo during OME.
source: However, they are unique in their N-terminal domains, and in that they are lipoproteins transferred with other cargo during OME.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: This is the first example of a polymorphic toxin system in which the toxin itself is a lipoprotein.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of a polymorphic toxin system in which the toxin itself is a lipoprotein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: SitA delivery likely only requires OM localization of the toxin and compatible TraA receptors.
source: Therefore, SitA delivery likely only requires OM localization of the toxin and compatible TraA receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the findings.

claim: The SitA toxin family constitutes a second identity constraint upon OME with partner cells.
source: Importantly, the SitA toxin family constitutes a second identity constraint upon OME with partner cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: For two cells to engage in OME, they must present compatible TraA receptors and contain immunity proteins to each other's toxins.
source: For two cells to engage in OME, not only must they present compatible TraA receptors, but they must also contain immunity proteins to each other's toxins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The finding that myxobacteria verify relatedness with sitAI confirms the notion that myxobacteria apply a bona fide kin discrimination mechanism during OME by requiring identity verification at multiple polymorphic loci.
source: The finding that myxobacteria verify relatedness with sitAI confirms the notion that myxobacteria apply a bona fide kin discrimination mechanism during OME by requiring identity verification at multiple polymorphic loci.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: SitA delivery range is restricted to within a single TraA recognition group.
source: SitA delivery range is restricted to within a single TraA recognition group.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: One of the primary functions of SitA is the discrimination of exchange partners.
source: This suggests that one of the primary functions of SitA is the discrimination of exchange partners, consistent with the notion that sharing large amounts of goods with non-kin is costly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Myxobacteria achieve safeguarding of OM material by inextricably linking the delivery of these goods with the delivery of SitA toxins.
source: Myxobacteria achieve this safeguard by inextricably linking the delivery of these goods with the delivery of SitA toxins.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Differential acquisition of antagonistic systems can affect cooperation compatibility between originally identical genotypes.
source: Differential acquisition of antagonistic systems can affect cooperation compatibility between originally identical genotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.
